title: Single Number (XOR)
description: XOR every value: pairs cancel to 0 and the loner survives. O(n) time, O(1) space.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: every value in `nums` appears exactly twice, except for one element that appears once. Return that loner. A few quick checks:"

• Is exactly one loner guaranteed, or could there be zero / multiple?
• Can values be negative or zero, or only positive integers?
• Any size bound on the array — is it always non-empty?
• Can I assume the values fit in JS's 32-bit bitwise range? (XOR on big ints behaves differently.)
sections.why: The 'exactly one loner, everything else paired' guarantee is what makes the XOR trick correct — if duplicates could appear three times, XOR would leave the triple instead of cancelling. Pinning that down before coding signals you understand WHICH problem structure makes the trick valid, not just that the trick exists. The negative-numbers check matters too: XOR works on the bit representation, so signed inputs are fine — but mentioning it shows you thought about it.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n) / O(n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is a hash map of counts: walk the array, increment `counts[n]` for each value, then scan the map for the entry with count 1 and return its key. That's O(n) time but O(n) space.

A second brute force is sort then scan pairs: after sorting, the loner is whichever element isn't equal to its neighbor. That's O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space if you sort in place."
sections.why: Two brute forces are worth naming because they expose the trade you're trying to beat: the hash-map version pays O(n) memory, the sort version pays O(n log n) time. The XOR solution beats both — O(n) time AND O(1) space — which is exactly the kind of 'is there a math/bit trick' question the interviewer is fishing for. Saying both candidates out loud makes the XOR leap feel earned rather than pulled from a hat.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to XOR?
sections.say:
"Three properties of XOR make this work, and the problem hands me all three: it's commutative (order doesn't matter), associative (grouping doesn't matter), and self-inverse — `a ^ a === 0`, and `a ^ 0 === a`. So if I fold all the values with XOR starting from 0, every paired value cancels itself out, and the loner — which has no partner to cancel with — survives. I never need to know WHICH value is the loner; the algebra figures it out for me."

"The trigger signal: 'find the unique element in a sea of pairs' plus an explicit ask for O(1) space. Whenever you see pairs-of-something plus a no-extra-space constraint, XOR cancellation is on the table."
sections.why: Naming the three properties — commutative, associative, self-inverse — is what distinguishes derivation from memorization. Saying 'XOR works because pairs cancel' is the right intuition but it's a one-liner; spelling out which algebraic property makes the cancellation order-independent is the answer that proves you understand WHY the loop works on an unsorted input. That's also what generalizes: the same algebra reappears in Missing Number, Single Number II/III, and Find the Duplicate.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me fold a couple of inputs to make sure the cancellation works the way I claimed." Three cases — a normal mix with the loner in the middle, a single-element degenerate, and a case where the loner comes last so you watch the running XOR settle to a non-zero value at the end.

examples.note: Classic mix — the loner (4) sits at the front, then two pairs cancel.
examples.trace:
result = 0          (0b0000)
n=4: result ^= 4 → 4 (0b0100)
n=1: result ^= 1 → 5 (0b0101)
n=2: result ^= 2 → 7 (0b0111)
n=1: result ^= 1 → 6 (0b0110)  — the 1-bit cancels
n=2: result ^= 2 → 4 (0b0100)  — the 2-bit cancels
return 4 ✓

examples.note: Single-element edge — one fold, one survivor.
Loner at the end — the running XOR transits 0 mid-loop, then ends at the loner.
examples.trace:
result = 0     (0b0000)
n=2: result ^= 2 → 2 (0b0010)
n=2: result ^= 2 → 0 (0b0000)  — pair cancelled
n=1: result ^= 1 → 1 (0b0001)
return 1 ✓

sections.why: The third example is the one worth narrating — the running XOR briefly returns to 0 after the pair cancels, then picks up the loner on the last step. That's the visual proof that the order of the inputs doesn't matter: the pair would have cancelled even if it was split by the loner. The second example also defends a real edge — a one-element input still works because `0 ^ x = x`, no special-case needed.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, edges worth flagging:"

• Single-element array → fold runs once, returns that value. ✓ (no special case needed thanks to the `a ^ 0 = a` identity)
• Negative numbers → XOR works on the underlying bit pattern, so signs are handled correctly. JS represents bitwise ops as signed int32, so `-1 ^ -1 === 0` just like for positives.
• Zero in the array → `0 ^ x = x`, so a zero pair cancels just like any other pair; a lone zero would correctly return 0.
• Values >= 2^31 — once you exceed signed int32 range, JS bitwise ops coerce to int32 and you lose precision on the high bits. If the problem allows large ints, mention BigInt XOR (`5n ^ 5n`) or that you'd want a guarantee they fit.
• Empty array — undefined behavior in most problem statements; fold returns 0, but I'd ask the interviewer rather than assume.
sections.why: The values-out-of-int32-range edge is the senior-tier touch most candidates miss. JS bitwise ops silently truncate to 32 signed bits — `(2**33) ^ 1` is just `1`, which is correct-looking but wrong for any input where the high bits actually matter. Flagging it shows you know the JS execution model, not just the algorithm. The zero-in-the-array call-out is the other one worth raising: it's the case where 'pairs cancel' and 'zero is the identity' visually overlap, and a careless implementation that special-cases zero would break.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — one pass, one XOR per element, each XOR is O(1).

Space is O(1) — a single accumulator integer, no auxiliary structure.

If you wanted to extend this: Single Number II (every value appears 3 times except one) breaks the pair-cancellation trick because three of the same value XORs to itself, not 0. The fix is to track each bit position mod 3 — either with two accumulators forming a state machine, or by scanning all 32 bit positions and counting set bits mod 3. Same algebraic spirit (the loner survives because of arithmetic, not bookkeeping), different finite-state setup."
sections.why: The O(1) space defense is the structural point — the trick is that the bit pattern of `result` literally IS the running parity of every bit position seen so far. There's no separate data structure because the integer itself encodes the count-mod-2 state for 32 independent bit slots in parallel. Naming Single Number II as the extension proves you see WHY pair-cancellation works (count mod 2) and where it breaks (count mod 3 needs a different state machine) — that's the kind of generalization-aware answer interviewers grade highly.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the XOR fold one value at a time. The state panel shows `result` in both decimal AND binary so you can watch matched pairs cancel bit-by-bit.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}`, state: { nums } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init result = 0 (XOR identity: a ^ 0 = a)', state: { nums, result: `0 (${bin(0)})` } };
yield { line: 4, label: `result ^= ${n} → ${prev} ^ ${n} = ${result}`, state: { nums, n: `${n} (${bin(n)})`, prev: `${prev} (${bin(prev)})`, result: `${result} (${bin(result)})` } };
yield { line: 5, label: `return ${result} (the loner — all paired bits cancelled to 0)`, state: { nums, result: `${result} (${bin(result)})`, returns: result } };

notes: XOR is commutative and associative — order does not matter; all pairs cancel.
a ^ a === 0 and a ^ 0 === a are the two identities that make this work.
No hash set needed — the bit pattern itself stores the running parity.

options: 0 is the identity for XOR (a ^ 0 === a)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the XOR single-number trick.

L3.prompt: Write `singleNumber(nums)` where every value appears twice except one — return the loner using XOR. O(n) time, O(1) space. Log `singleNumber([4, 1, 2, 1, 2])`.
hints: XOR with itself = 0; XOR with 0 = unchanged.
Fold the array with ^= starting from 0.
